course_description:
This course introduces the institutions, rules and principles of Public International Law. It explores the history, theory and efficacy of the international legal system as well as the system's sources of law and its general rules and principles. It also introduces specific areas of international legal regulation.

The early 2000s saw increasing interdependence of entities (such as nation States, corporations and human beings) that are separated by national borders. More recently, attempts to acquire territory by the aggressive use of military force and the withdrawal of support for other international legal standards and for international institutions have challenged assumptions upon which such interdependence was based. International law has long been used to ensure coexistence and cooperation amongst States separated by national borders. International law has also been used to achieve levels of legal integration in certain parts of the world and between particular States. Since the end of the Second World War international law has also reflected a commitment to certain substantive values . As States and other entities struggle to maintain their commitment to these values in an interdependent world, international law is seen as important to both the enjoyment of the benefits of increased interdependence and the avoidance of dangers inherent in the process.

course_aims:
Education Mission Statement

The mission of the School of Law is to educate you in and about the law. We seek to assist you to think critically about the law and to investigate its structures, principles, policies, and values. This is achieved by engaging with you as fellow investigators in a range of critical and intellectual conversations about the law and its place in society. Our role is thus to guide you in your own intellectual journey in the law and to equip you with the necessary skills that will enable you to continue that journey long after you have left the School.

Resolve or provide legally defensible solutions to theoretical and/or practical questions arising from the application of the rules and principles of international law.
Critically evaluate the most important approaches that are suggested by legal scholars when dealing with problems of international law.

learning_activities.learning_period: Multiple weeks From Week 1 To Week 13 (27 Jul - 01 Nov)
learning_activities.topic: Lectures The programme for lectures and tutorials is set out in the course Blackboard site (Learn.UQ). The lecture topics are: Introduction to international law I - Basic features; Introduction to international law II - Institutions and efficacy (and comparisons with Australian law); Introduction to international law III - Historical and theoretical issues; Sources of international law I - The sources of international legal obligations and rights (introduction to treaties, custom and general principles of law); Sources of international law II - The sources of international legal obligations and rights (custom, general principles of law, unilaterally assumed obligations, subsidiary sources and soft law); Sources of international law III - The law of treaties; International law and national law - How different national legal systems view international law; The subjects of international law I - States and intergovernmental organisations - personality, capacity and responsibility; The subjects of international law II - Natural persons - the protection of human rights under international law; The subjects of international law III - Natural persons and corporate entities - individual criminal responsibility under international law, and international economic law; Specialised areas of international law I - International environmental law, and international law of the sea, air and outer space; and Specialised areas of international law II and concluding observations - Use of force and the law of armed conflict, and concluding discussion of international law. Learning outcomes: L01, L02, L03

learning_activities.learning_period: Multiple weeks From Week 2 To Week 13 (03 Aug - 01 Nov)
learning_activities.topic: Tutorials The tutorial topics are: Introduction to international law and a consideration of whether International Law is really law; Institutional issues and theoretical critiques of international law; Treaties, customary international law and peremptory norms; General principles, unilateral declarations, judicial decisions and the writings of eminent publicists; The law of treaties; Australian Law and International Law; States and intergovernmental organisations; International Law and natural persons - International human rights law; Specialised areas of international law - International economic law, international environmental law and the law of the sea; Reflections on the entire course. Learning outcomes: L01, L02, L03
